opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real tension, and I think about it a lot, partly from the research side and partly from the company side.

On one hand, starting with one or two customers who have a very real, very painful problem is often the best thing you can do. You get incredibly concrete feedback. You're not designing for some imagined average user; you're watching someone actually try to get their work done and seeing exactly where it breaks. A lot of the systems work I've been involved in started that way. You had a small number of people with a workload that existing tools just couldn't handle, and solving it for them forced you to get the fundamentals right.

The risk, of course, is that you overfit. You end up building something that's really a custom consulting project with a product label on it. Every feature request from that one big customer feels urgent, and if you just say yes to everything, a year later you have a product that works great for them and is confusing or irrelevant for everyone else.

So the way I'd weigh it is to ask a few questions. First, is their problem a leading indicator? Are they hitting this because they're a bit ahead of where the rest of the market is going, in terms of data scale, or how they're using models, or whatever it is? If so, building for them is actually building for the future. If they're just weird, that's a different story.

Second, can you separate the general abstraction from their specific requirements? When a customer asks for something, I try to understand the underlying need and ask whether there's a more general primitive that solves their case and also ten other people's. That's usually where the good design comes from.

And third, you want to be deliberately talking to a broader set of users early, even if they're not paying yet. Open source is really useful here, because you get signals from a lot of people you'd never have found otherwise, and that keeps you honest about whether you're building something general.

So I wouldn't say avoid it. Some focus on a few demanding customers is healthy. You just have to be disciplined about which of their requests are telling you something about the world and which are just about them.

r001.rationale: The response describes concrete benefits of starting with a few customers and cautions against overfitting, but it does not judge the upside to be much greater than the downside.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the risk of overfitting but does not compare it with overly broad product scope or say broad scope is the bigger problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a lot early on at Databricks, and honestly it's a tension I think every infrastructure company runs into. The risk is real. If you build around one or two customers, you can end up with a product that's really a consulting project in disguise. You've solved their problem, they're happy, and then you go to the next company and nothing transfers because you optimized for the idiosyncrasies of one environment.

But I'd push back a little on treating it purely as a risk, because the alternative, building in the abstract for some imagined average user, is usually worse. With Spark, a lot of what made it work was that we were sitting with actual people at Berkeley and in the early days at companies trying to run real workloads, and we could see where they got stuck. You learn things that way you would never guess from a whiteboard.

So the way I'd frame it is: the question isn't how many customers, it's whether the problem they have is one you believe lots of other people have, and whether you're disciplined about separating the general thing from the specific thing. When a customer asks for a feature, the exercise is to ask, what's the underlying need here, and is there a version of this that ten other companies would also want? If you can answer that, one or two design partners is actually a great position to be in. You get fast feedback and you get someone who'll tell you the truth.

Where it goes wrong is when the economics take over. If one customer is most of your revenue, their roadmap becomes your roadmap, and it's very hard to say no. So I'd say pick design partners deliberately, make sure they're representative of a market you actually want, and try to get to three or four fairly quickly so you can see what's common across them. The pattern across a handful of users is much more informative than the full detail of any one.

r001.rationale: The response calls one or two design partners a great position for fast feedback, but it does not judge that upside to be much greater than the downside of overfitting.

r002.rationale: It says building for an imagined average user can be worse, but it does not compare overfitting with pursuing an overly broad product scope.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether those customers are representative of a broader problem. One or two customers can be incredibly valuable because you can work closely with them, understand what they actually need, and see whether your product makes a difference. The risk is that you end up building something that only makes sense inside their particular organization.

So I’d start with that close collaboration, but also talk to other potential users. Do they recognize the problem? How are they solving it today? You don’t necessarily need them all to adopt the product immediately, but you want evidence that the need extends beyond those first customers.

r001.rationale: The response recognizes the value of working closely with one or two customers and the risk of overfitting, but does not judge the upside to be much greater than the downside.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the risk of building for only one organization, but does not compare that risk with overly broad product scope or say which is the bigger problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether those customers are representative of a broader market. One or two customers can be incredibly valuable if they have a real problem, they’re willing to work closely with you, and you have reason to believe other people will run into the same thing. The risk is that you end up building something very specific to how one company operates.

So I’d use those customers to get fast feedback, but I’d also talk to other potential users. Do they recognize the problem? Are they trying to solve it themselves? You don’t need everyone to agree on the exact feature set, but you want evidence that the underlying need exists beyond those first customers.

r001.rationale: It describes potential value in working closely with one or two customers and the risk of building too specifically, but does not judge the upside to be much greater than that downside.

r002.rationale: It discusses validating the need beyond initial customers, but makes no comparison between product scope that is too broad and overfitting to those customers.
